The Health in the Americas+1 country profiles are based on the interagency indicators available as of the dates referenced. The sources are referenced [in this table](https://hia.paho.org/en/countries-22/sources). In some cases, the values of the indicators may differ from the most recent data available in the country.

## Environmental and social determinants of health

In 2000 the total population of Peru was 26 598 331 inhabitants; by 2024 this figure had risen to 34 217 848, representing a 28.6% increase. Regarding the country’s demographic profile, in 2024 people over 65 years of age accounted for 9.2% of the total population, an increase of 4.9 percentage points compared to the year 2000. In 2024, there were 101.1 women per 100 men and 38.5 older people (65 years or older) per 100 children under 15 years of age, as can be seen in the country’s population pyramids, distributed by age group and sex (Figure 1). Considering the population between 15 and 64 years of age to be potentially active (i.e., potential participants in the labor force), this group represented 66.8% of the total population of the country in 2024 (22 858 026 people). When we add these figures to the potentially passive population (8 202 157 under 15 years of age and 3 157 665 over 65 years of age), the result is a dependency ratio of 49.7 potentially passive people per 100 potentially active people. This ratio was 64.0 in 2000.

Life expectancy at birth in 2024 was 77.9 years, higher than the average for the Region of the Americas and 8.1 years higher that in 2000 (69.8).

###### Figure 1. Population pyramids of Peru, years 2000 and 2024

Between 2004 and 2018, the average number of years of schooling in Peru increased by 13.5%, reaching an average of 9.8 years in the latest year for which information is available. The unemployment rate in 2023 was 3.5%. Disaggregated by sex, the rate was 4.2% for women and 2.9% for men. The literacy rate was 99.3% in 2022. In men, this figure was 99.3%; in women, 99.3%. In addition, 27.5% of the population were below the national poverty line in 2022, a decrease from 58.7% in 2004. In 2022, 2.7% of the population was living in poverty, defined as the percentage of the population with an income of less than US$ 2.15 per day; this is below the regional average of 2.6%.

During the period 2000-2022, the country improved its score on the Human Development Index, with an increase of 12.9% (from a score of 0.675 to a score of 0.762); during the same period, the index rose 14.6% internationally and 11.2% in Latin America (Figure 2).

###### Figure 2. Human Development Index in the Region of the Americas, 2022

In 2021, public expenditure on health accounted for 3.99% of gross domestic product (GDP) (Figure 3) and 16.94% of total public expenditure, while out-of-pocket spending on health accounted for 27.22% of total health expenditure.

###### Figure 3. Domestic general government health expenditure as percentage of gross domestic product, 2021

## Digital coverage

In 2021, 71.1% of the population had an internet connection, representing a considerable increase from 2000, when 3.1% of the population had an internet connection.

## Health situation

#### Maternal and child health

Between 2002 and 2022, infant mortality in Peru increased from 16 to 17 deaths per 1000 live births, a decrease of 6.3% (Figure 4). The percentage of low-weight births (less than 2500 g) decreased from 8.4% to 6.6% between 2004 and 2022, while exclusive breastfeeding in the child population up to 6 months of age was 67.2% in 2000 and 69.9% in 2009 (latest available data).

Regarding the immunization strategy, measles vaccination coverage was 74% in 2022, a decrease of 23 percentage points from 2000.

###### Figure 4. Infant mortality per 1000 live births, 1996–2022

The maternal mortality ratio in 2020 was estimated at 68.5 deaths per 100 000 live births, representing a 39.5% reduction compared to the estimated value in 2000 (Figure 5). In relation to fertility, it is estimated that in 2024 women had an average of 2.0 children throughout their reproductive lives. In the specific case of adolescent fertility, there was a 41.6% decrease, from 73.5 live births per 1000 women aged 15 to 19 years in 2000 to 42.9 in 2024. In 2022, 98.6% of births were attended by skilled birth personnel. Between 2000 and 2020 the percentage of pregnant people who had four or more consultations for antenatal care increased from 69% to 88.4%.

###### Figure 5. Maternal mortality per 100 000 live births, 2000–2020

#### Communicable diseases

In 2022, there were 83 new cases of tuberculosis per 100 000 population in Peru. In 2019, the overall tuberculosis mortality rate (age-adjusted and per 100 000 population) was 7.1 (4.3 in women and 10.1 in men).

In 2022, the estimated human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection incidence rate (new diagnoses) was 27.2 per 100 000 population. The age-adjusted mortality rate for HIV was 2.6 per 100 000 population in 2019. It should be noted that during the 2000-2019 period this indicator decreased by 88.3%. There was one reported case of human rabies in the country in 2022.

#### Noncommunicable diseases and risk factors

In Peru in 2023, the prevalence of tobacco use among people aged 15 and older was 6.6%. In the same age group, the prevalence of overweight and obesity was 68.1% in 2022.

In 2015, the reported prevalence of arterial hypertension (high blood pressure) among people aged 18 years or older was 13.7%, a decrease of six percentage points compared to 2000 (19.7%). The prevalence of diabetes mellitus, which stood at 6.7% in 2000, increased to 7.7% in 2014.

## Mortality

In 2019, the adjusted rate of potentially preventable premature mortality in Peru was 153.7 deaths per 100 000 population, a decrease of 40.2% compared to the rate of 257.2 in 2000. This meant that, in 2019, the rate in the country was 32.2% lower than the average rate reported for the Region of the Americas as a whole. Among potentially preventable premature deaths, the rate for preventable causes was 83.3 per 100 000 population in 2019, which is 39.2% lower than the regional average rate; and the rate for treatable causes was 70.3 per 100 000 population, below the regional average of 89.6.

The overall age-adjusted mortality rate was 4.2 per 1000 population in 2019, a decrease of 30.2% compared to 2000 (six deaths per 1000 population).

When deaths are categorized into three main groups, it is observed that, in 2019, the age-adjusted mortality rate from communicable diseases was 73.5 per 100 000 population (79.9 per 100 000 in men and 66.8 per 100 000 in women), while the age-adjusted mortality rate from noncommunicable diseases was 303.8 per 100 000 population (327.2 per 100 000 in men and 282.6 per 100 000 in women). The rate of age-adjusted mortality from external causes was 42.4 per 100 000 population (63.9 per 100 000 in men and 21.2 per 100 000 in women), including road traffic accidents (13.4 per 100 000 population), homicides (9.1 per 100 000 population) and suicides (2.7 per 100 000 population). In 2000, the percentage distribution of causes was 55.3% for noncommunicable diseases, 33.0% for communicable diseases, and 11.6% for external causes; in 2019, the percentages were 72.6%, 17.5%, and 9.9%, respectively (Figure 6).

###### Figure 6. Proportional mortality in Peru, 2000 and 2019

#### Cancer mortality

Regarding cancer mortality from tumors, in 2019, the adjusted mortality rate from prostate cancer was 20.5 per 100 000 men; lung cancer, 10.2 per 100 000; and colorectal cancer, 9 per 100 000. In women, these values were 11.6 deaths per 100 000 for breast cancer, 9.3 per 100 000 for lung cancer, and 6.8 per 100 000 for colorectal cancer.

Country COVID-19 Perspective
## The health situation and the COVID-19 pandemic

In the Region of the Americas, Peru ranked first in terms of the number of deaths from COVID-19 in 2020, a ranking it maintained in 2021. In 2022 it ranked 16th, with a cumulative figure of 6418.4 deaths per million population for the three years (Figure 7).

According to estimates by the World Health Organization, there was a total of 133 815 excess deaths in 2020, or 406 per 100 000 population. A total of 155 852 deaths were estimated in 2021, for an excess mortality rate of 467 per 100 000.

As of 31 December 2021, at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine had been given to 87.9% of the country's population. As of 20 April 2022 (latest available data), 81% of the population had completed the vaccination schedule. The vaccination campaign began on 20 February 2021, and three types of COVID-19 vaccine have been used to date.

###### Figure 7. Cumulative COVID-19 deaths in the Region of the Americas, to July 29th, 2023

## Prospects

#### Measures to achieve universal health coverage

Law No. 30 885, which was approved in 2018, establishes the creation and operation of Integrated Health Networks, which became regulated in 2020, thus instituting the necessary mechanisms for monitoring, supervising, and evaluating them.

In January 2020, the Technical Document Life Course Model of Comprehensive Health Care for the Person, the Family, and the Community (MCI) was approved. A few months later, approval was given to the National Multisectoral Health Policy for 2030: “Peru, Healthy Country,” by which the State committed, over the following ten years, to implement measures to promote healthier behaviors, improve access to health systems, and reduce the social and economic vulnerability of the population. This initiative involves 13 sectors and is overseen by the Ministry of Health.

The following year, in July 2021, the Technical Document National Plan for the Implementation of Integrated Health Networks was approved.

Lastly, the General Government Policy for the period 2021–2026, approved in October 2021, contains ten priority axes and lines of intervention to overcome barriers to the effective and equal exercise of people’s fundamental rights, including the right to health.

#### Challenges related to population health

One of Peru’s main challenges is to remedy the segmentation and fragmentation of health services, a situation that the government has tried to address by establishing integrated health networks; 91 of these have been structured (the entities that constitute them have been identified), and 75 are operational.

Another major challenge is to reduce Peruvians’ out-of-pocket spending on health coverage and health care. According to the National Household Survey (ENAHO) 2020, during the pandemic, people without any type of health insurance who experienced symptoms of COVID-19 reported spending 45% more than people with some form of health insurance.

A third challenge for national health policy is to increase public spending on health (3.3% of GDP in 2018) to reach the medium-term target of 6% by 2030, which was set for the countries of the Region of the Americas in the Sustainable Health Agenda for the Americas 2018–2030.

The pandemic has had a negative impact on various health indicators, many of which are used to monitor the Sustainable Development Goals. These indicators include maternal mortality and morbidity, particularly among the indigenous population and the dispersed rural population; infant mortality, caused by premature birth and low birth weight; anemia; and vaccine-preventable diseases. Also notable is the high prevalence of overweight and obesity, a condition that especially affects children.

#### COVID-19 pandemic response

As in many other parts of the world, the COVID-19 pandemic in Peru has provided important lessons, which should be reviewed in the short and medium term to guide the health policies and actions needed in the coming years.

At the same time, the public policy response to the pandemic had the effect of improving various aspects of people's access to health services and health care, including the following:

*   The number of human resources for health, primarily medical and nursing professionals, was increased.
*   More than 2500 beds were added in intensive care units (ICUs).
*   The national supply of oxygen was increased through development of oxygen generating plants and by providing oxygen concentrators throughout the country.
*   First-level care was strengthened by implementing temporary care centers.
*   Stocks of necessary personal protective equipment and supplies, as well as medicines and ICU kits, were secured.
*   The National Laboratory Network for the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 was strengthened.
*   Essential services were restored.
*   Health promotion and primary health care activities were promoted.
*   The work of community health workers—people from the various communities who conduct a variety of activities to promote healthy communities—was strengthened nationwide.
*   Telemedicine was promoted and developed at different levels of health care.

Pending tasks include improving health infrastructure, strengthening the work of integrated health networks and at the primary care level, and reactivating priority public health programs.

#### Measures to reduce inequalities in health

Efforts to address health inequalities are being carried out under the _General Government Policy for 2021–2026_, which contains ten key areas with priority guidelines and lines of intervention to guide public entities working to eliminate these gaps.

The first of these keys areas promotes social welfare through food security, with a line of action to develop “a universal, unified, free, decentralized, and participatory health system.”

Similarly, the _National Multisectoral Health Policy for 2030: “Peru, Healthy Country”_ sets forth three objectives:

1.   Promote healthier habits, behaviors, and lifestyles in the population.
2.   Ensure people's access to timely, quality, comprehensive health services.
3.   Improve the living conditions that create vulnerability and health risks.

All these normative instruments, as well as the manual for implementing the _Life Course Model of Comprehensive Health Care for the Person, the Family, and the Community,_ approved in February 2021, establish national strategies to reduce health inequalities and address the social determinants of health throughout the life course, in addition to allocating the resources needed to maintain the entire health system.

#### Agreement between Peru and the United Nations System

The signing of the _United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework: Peru 2022-2026_ focuses on bringing the country into alignment with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals. Its purpose is to incorporate these guidelines and goals into national policies, through a work plan with five central strategic priorities: social development, environmental sustainability, economic development, democratic governance, and security.

# World Population Dashboard

![Image 20: World Population Dashboard](https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/unfpa_global_sowp_portal/images/worldpop_dashboard_intro_image.jpg)

The World Population Dashboard showcases global population data, including fertility rate, gender parity in school enrolment, information on sexual and reproductive health, and much more. Together, these data shine a light on the health and rights of people around the world, especially women and young people. The numbers here come from UNFPA and fellow UN agencies, and are updated annually.

**DEFINITIONS OF THE INDICATORS**  
 Maternal mortality ratio: Number of maternal deaths during a given time period per 100,000 live births during the same time period. (SDG indicator 3.1.1)  
 Births attended by skilled health personnel: Percentage of births attended by skilled heath personnel (doctor, nurse or midwife). (SDG indicator 3.1.2)  
 Number of new HIV infections, all ages, per 1,000 uninfected population: Number of new HIV infections per 1000 person-years among the uninfected population. (SDG indicator 3.3.1)  
 Contraceptive prevalence rate: Percentage of women aged 15 to 49 years who are currently using any method of contraception.  
 Contraceptive prevalence rate, modern method: Percentage of women aged 15 to 49 years who are currently using any modern method of contraception.  
 Unmet need for family planning: Percentage of women aged 15 to 49 years who want to stop or delay childbearing but are not using a method of contraception.  
 Proportion of demand satisfied with modern methods: Percentage of total demand for family planning among women aged 15 to 49 years that is satisfied by the use of modern contraception. (SDG indicator 3.7.1)  
 Laws and regulations that guarantee access to sexual and reproductive health care, information and education: The extent to which countries have national laws and regulations that guarantee full and equal access to women and men aged 15 years and older to sexual and reproductive health care, information and education. (SDG indicator 5.6.2)  
 Universal health coverage (UHC) service coverage index: Average coverage of essential services based on tracer interventions that include reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health, infectious diseases, non-communicable diseases and service capacity and access, among the general and the most disadvantaged population. (SDG indicator 3.8.1)  
 Adolescent birth rate: Number of births per 1,000 adolescent girls aged 15–19. (SDG indicator 3.7.2)  
 Child marriage by age 18: Proportion of women aged 20-24 years who were married or in a union before age 18. (SDG indicator 5.3.1)  
 Female genital mutilation prevalence among girls aged 15-49: Proportion of girls aged 15-49 years who have undergone female genital mutilation. (SDG indicator 5.3.2)  
 Intimate partner violence, past 12 months: Percentage of ever-partnered women and girls aged 15 to 49 who have experienced physical and/or sexual partner violence in the previous 12 months. (SDG indicator 5.2.1)  
 Decision making on sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights: Percentage of women aged 15-49 years who are married (or in union), who make their own decisions on three areas – their healthcare, use of contraception, and sexual intercourse with their partners. (SDG indicator 5.6.1).  
 Decision making on women's own health care: Percentage of women aged 15-49 years who are married (or in union), who make their own decisions on their healthcare. (SDG indicator 5.6.1).  
 Decision making on contraceptive use: Percentage of women aged 15-49 years who are married (or in union), who make their own decisions on use of contraception. (SDG indicator 5.6.1).  
 Decision making on sexual intercourse: Percentage of women aged 15-49 years who are married (or in union), who make their own decisions on sexual intercourse with their partners. (SDG indicator 5.6.1).  
 Total net enrolment rate, primary education: Total number of students of the official age group for primary education who are enrolled in any level of education, expressed as a percentage of the corresponding population.  
 Gender parity index, total net enrolment rate, primary education: Ratio of female to male values of total net enrolment rate for primary education.  
 Total net enrolment rate, lower secondary education: Total number of students of the official age group for lower secondary education who are enrolled in any level of education, expressed as a percentage of the corresponding population.  
 Gender parity index, total net enrolment rate, lower secondary education: Ratio of female to male values of total net enrolment rate for lower secondary education.  
 Total net enrolment rate, upper secondary education: Total number of students of the official age group for upper secondary education who are enrolled in any level of education, expressed as a percentage of the corresponding population.  
 Gender parity index, total net enrolment rate, upper secondary education: Ratio of female to male values of total net enrolment rate for upper secondary education.  
 Total population: Estimated size of national populations at mid-year.  
 Population annual doubling time, years: The number of years required for the total population to double in size if the annual rate of population change would remain constant. It is calculated as ln(2)/r where r is the annual population growth rate. Doubling time is computed only for fast growing populations with growth rates exceeding 0.5 per cent.  
 Population aged 0-14, percent: Proportion of the population between age 0 and age 14.  
 Population aged 10-19, percent: Proportion of the population between age 10 and age 19.  
 Population aged 10-24, percent: Proportion of the population between age 10 and age 24.  
 Population aged 15-64, percent: Proportion of the population between age 15 and age 64.  
 Population aged 65 and older, percent: Proportion of the population aged 65 and older.  
 Total fertility rate: Number of children who would be born per woman if she lived to the end of her childbearing years and bore children at each age in accordance with prevailing age-specific fertility rates.  
 Life expectancy at birth: Number of years newborn children would live if subject to the mortality risks prevailing for the cross section of population at the time of their birth.

# World Population Dashboard

![Image 20: World Population Dashboard](https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/unfpa_global_sowp_portal/images/worldpop_dashboard_intro_image.jpg)

The World Population Dashboard showcases global population data, including fertility rate, gender parity in school enrolment, information on sexual and reproductive health, and much more. Together, these data shine a light on the health and rights of people around the world, especially women and young people. The numbers here come from UNFPA and fellow UN agencies, and are updated annually.

**DEFINITIONS OF THE INDICATORS**  
 Maternal mortality ratio: Number of maternal deaths during a given time period per 100,000 live births during the same time period. (SDG indicator 3.1.1)

Life expectancy at birth, women

* * *

Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live, if the prevailing patterns of mortality at the time of her/his birth were to stay the same throughout her/his life. Life expectancy at 65 is the average number of years a person at the age of 65 is expected to live, if the prevailing patterns of mortality at the time when she/he has reached the age of 65 were to stay the same throughout the rest of her/his life.

Life expectancy at birth, women

* * *

Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live, if the prevailing patterns of mortality at the time of her/his birth were to stay the same throughout her/his life. Life expectancy at 65 is the average number of years a person at the age of 65 is expected to live, if the prevailing patterns of mortality at the time when she/he has reached the age of 65 were to stay the same throughout the rest of her/his life.

## Abstract

### Background

Maternal mortality is a global public health priority, with the Sustainable Development Agenda and the Sustainable Health Agenda for the Americas setting ambitious targets for its reduction by 2030. Despite progress in poverty reduction and increased life expectancy, Peru faces urgent health challenges, including persistently high maternal mortality, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. To analyze maternal mortality trends and epidemiological characteristics in Peru, explore its determinants during 2010–2021, and quantify its inequalities before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

### Methods

An ecological study used administrative data from the 25 Peruvian regions (2010–2021). Maternal mortality ratio (MMR) trends and key characteristics were analyzed. A mixed-effects negative binomial regression model assessed associations between MMR and proximal (e.g., skilled birth attendance [SBA]) and distal (e.g., unmet basic needs [UBN]) determinants. Inequality trends in MMR and SBA coverage were evaluated using standard metrics.

### Results

MMR declined from 82.0 to 55.6 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births between 2010 and 2019 but rose to 86.7 in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Excess maternal mortality during 2020–2021 (44.8%) was concentrated among older mothers, primiparas, and those without prenatal care, with indirect causes playing a major role. The reduction in MMR (2010–2019) correlated with decreased UBN and increased SBA. Ecosocial inequalities in MMR remained significant, with maternal mortality disproportionately affecting regions with higher UBN (78.7, 85.3, and 75.3 excess deaths per 100,000 live births in 2010–2014, 2015–2019, and 2020–2021, respectively). SBA coverage improved nationally, narrowing regional inequalities from a 30.6-point deficit in 2012 to 14.9 in 2021.

### Conclusions

Maternal mortality in Peru declined significantly before 2020, but the COVID-19 pandemic reversed this progress, with MMR rising to pre-2010 levels. Ecosocial inequalities persist, disproportionately affecting disadvantaged regions. However, SBA coverage improvements highlight the impact of proximal determinant interventions. Strengthened social reforms targeting distal determinants are crucial to reducing maternal mortality and inequalities in Peru.

## Background

Maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is one of the key indicators of public health, reflecting the overall effectiveness, accessibility, and equity of health systems. Reducing maternal mortality has been a global priority for decades. The third Sustainable Development Goal of the 2030 Agenda aims to reduce the MMR to less than 70 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births globally by 2030 [1]. In the Americas, the Sustainable Health Agenda 2018–2030 has adopted an even more ambitious target of less than 30 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030, with an explicit focus on closing equity gaps that disproportionately affect the most vulnerable women [2].

Despite these commitments, recent estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO) indicate that maternal mortality has hardly declined since 2015. At the current pace, the world is off track to meet the established goal, and the global MMR would be more than double the SDG target [3]. This critical situation is mirrored in the Americas region [4]. National averages often obscure significant social and health inequalities. Studies in some countries in the Americas have explored trends and inequalities in maternal mortality and its proximal determinants– such as prenatal care, skilled birth attendance, and postnatal care– using spatially disaggregated administrative data and/or surveys. These studies invariably reveal profound and persistent socioeconomic inequalities in maternal mortality, even amidst national-level improvements in the MMR [5,6,7,8].

In Peru, maternal mortality remains a serious public health concern, particularly among socially disadvantaged populations [9, 10]. Social inequalities, such as poverty, rural residence, and ethnic background, continue to restrict equitable access to essential maternal health services. The COVID-19 pandemic has further exacerbated these inequalities [11], directly through increased maternal morbidity and mortality related to infection [12], and indirectly through widespread disruptions in maternal health services [13]. These disruptions have likely amplified preexisting barriers to care, including lack of transportation, shortages of trained personnel in rural and Amazonian regions, and financial constraints.

Although Peru achieved substantial progress during the Millennium Development Goals era, reducing its national MMR from 88.5 per 100,000 live births in 2001–2003 to 68.7 in 2012–2015, and narrowing regional inequality gaps by over 50%, significant disparities persisted [14]. In the context of COVID-19, the extent to which these inequalities have widened or changed remains insufficiently studied.

Despite persistent inequalities and the recent disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, there is still a lack of updated and systematic analyses in Peru that assess how the key epidemiological patterns and inequities in maternal mortality have evolved over time. This study aims to describe the trends and key epidemiological characteristics of maternal mortality in Peru, ecologically explore its determinants during 2010–2021, and quantify inequalities within the country before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

## Methods

### Study design, variables, and data sources

This study employed a case series and ecological design. The case series included individual records of maternal deaths from the epidemiological surveillance system of Peru’s National Center for Epidemiology, Prevention and Disease Control (CDC-Peru). Maternal death was defined as the death of a woman of reproductive age (15–49 years) while pregnant or within 42 days of pregnancy termination, regardless of the pregnancy duration or location, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes [15, 16]. Case series variables included calendar year, age, education level, cause of death, ethnicity, occupation, prenatal care, birth plan, and primigravidity.

The MMR was defined as the ratio of maternal deaths to live births in the country, region, or specific geographic area during a given calendar period, expressed per 100,000 live births. Annual estimates of MMR and maternal deaths at the national and subnational levels (regional territories) were calculated using the capture-recapture method [17], incorporating data from Peru’s epidemiological surveillance system and vital statistics registry. COVID-19–related mortality analysis utilized data from the CDC-Peru epidemiological surveillance system. For the classification of indirect maternal deaths associated with COVID-19, the technical criteria established for the identification of COVID-19–related deaths were applied in accordance with WHO recommendations [18, 19].

The ecological analysis considered the 25 territorial regions of Peru as the units of analysis. Variables included in the exploratory analysis – besides calendar year, live births, and MMR – were the proportion of women of reproductive age using modern contraceptive methods (MCM), the proportion of adolescent mothers or first-time pregnant adolescents (AFP), and skilled birth attendance (SBA) as proximal determinants of maternal mortality. Additionally, the prevalence of unmet basic needs (UBN) and gross domestic product (GDP) per capita were included as distal determinants. Data on MCM, AFP, and SBA were obtained from official reports published by Peru’s National Institute of Statistics and Informatics (INEI), derived from the Demographic and Health Survey (ENDES) [20]. ENDES is a nationally representative survey that uses a complex, stratified, multistage sampling design based on household self-reports. SBA was defined as the proportion of live births attended by qualified health personnel (physician, obstetrician, or nurse), and INEI reported no changes in its definition for the period 2010–2021. Data on UBN and GDP were obtained from publicly available official estimates provided by INEI.

### Data analysis

Trends in annual national estimates of MMR and its proximal and distal determinants from 2010 to 2021 were analyzed. The epidemiological characteristics of maternal deaths during the pandemic biennium (2020–2021) were compared with those of the pre-pandemic biennium (2018–2019) using chi-squared or Fisher’s exact tests, depending on sample size and expected frequencies. Additionally, for each variable category, the proportional excess maternal mortality during the pandemic biennium was calculated using the standard formula analogous to the attributable fraction:

$$\begin{array}{l}\:excess\:maternal\:deaths\:\left(\%\right)\:=\\\:\frac{\left({{deaths}_{pandemic}\:-\:{deaths}_{prepandemic}}_{}\right)}{{deaths}_{prepandemic}}\times\:100\end{array}$$

A mixed-effects negative binomial regression model was used to examine the ecological association between MMR and proximal and distal determinants for the 2010–2019 period, excluding pandemic years to avoid disruptions in MMR trends. The multivariable analysis included random effects for region and year to control for unobserved variability. Prior to model fitting, we assessed multicollinearity among explanatory variables using the variance inflation factor (VIF), computed from an ordinary least squares regression model. Predictors with VIF values greater than 5 were reviewed for potential redundancy. SBA, identified a priori as a key variable, was retained in the final model after confirming its VIF was within acceptable limits and that its inclusion did not compromise model stability (Additional file 1, Table S5).

Inequality analyses utilized UBN as an equity stratifier. A household is considered poor by UBN if it meets at least one of the following criteria: (1) inadequate housing conditions, based on wall and floor materials and housing type; (2) overcrowding, defined as more than 3.4 persons per room; (3) lack of any type of sanitation; (4) presence of at least one child aged 6–12 not attending school; or (5) high economic dependency, defined as households with a head of household with incomplete primary education (up to second grade) and either (i) four or more persons per employed household member, or (ii) no employed members at all [21, 22]. Regional MMR data were consolidated into three periods (2010–2014, 2015–2019, and 2020–2021) for stability, while SBA data corresponded to 2012, 2017, and 2021. Four standard inequality summary metrics were calculated: absolute gap, relative gap, slope index of inequality (SII), and concentration index of inequality (CIx), following WHO’s established methodology [23]. The absolute gap represents the difference between the weighted mean of the most disadvantaged quintile and that of the most advantaged; higher values indicate greater absolute inequality, while values close to zero reflect greater equity. The relative gap was presented as a ratio between these same quintiles; values greater than 1 indicate a disproportionate burden in the most disadvantaged group, while values less than 1 reflect a greater burden in the most advantaged group. The SII, estimated through weighted regression, represents the absolute difference in the health indicator between the most advantaged extreme (social position 1) and the most disadvantaged (social position 0); a negative value indicates that the health indicator is higher in regions with worse social position, while a positive value indicates a greater burden in the more advantaged regions. The CIx summarizes the relative inequality across the entire distribution of the stratifier, where negative values indicate concentration of the health indicator in the most disadvantaged regions, and positive values in the most advantaged [24]. The SII was calculated using weighted regression with a negative binomial model for MMR and a logistic model for SBA, as these models showed better fit based on mean squared error. Data analyses were performed using the R programming language, version 4 [25].

### Ethical considerations

This study did not involve human participants; only secondary, anonymized, and publicly accessible data were used. Therefore, ethical committee approval was not sought.

## Results

### Trends in maternal mortality and its determinants

Figure 1 illustrates the trends in the MMR and some of its proximal and distal determinants from 2010 to 2021. Between 2010 and 2019, the estimated MMR in Peru exhibited a declining trend, dropping from 82 to 55.6 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, with a marked reduction between 2015 and 2016 (from 76.5 to 59.7). Prior to the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in 2015, the MMR decreased by 8% during 2010–2014, with an average annual reduction rate of 1.6%. Subsequently, a more significant reduction of 20.9% was observed between 2015 and 2019, with an average annual reduction rate of 4.18%. However, this trend reversed during the pandemic years, with the MMR rising to 86.7 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2021 (Fig.1A). A similar pattern was observed in the trends for adolescent pregnancy (Fig.1C) and UBN (Fig.1F). In contrast, SBA (Fig.1B), modern contraceptive prevalence (Fig.1D), and GDP per capita (Fig.1E) showed upward trends during the same period, with a temporary decline in 2020 (and SBA in 2021).

### Epidemiological profile of maternal mortality and excess mortality during the pandemic

The proportional distribution of maternal deaths by age, education level, ethnicity, occupation, prenatal care, birth plan, and gravidity was statistically identical between the pre-pandemic biennium (2018–2019) and the pandemic biennium (2020–2021). Overall, maternal mortality was concentrated among women aged 30–39 years, with low education levels, of Mestizo ethnicity, in unpaid occupations, receiving prenatal care, lacking a birth plan, and multiparous. Hypertensive disorders and obstetric hemorrhages were the leading direct causes of maternal death in both periods, accounting for 76.3% and 77.9% of direct causes, respectively. Deaths linked to COVID-19 infection represented 56.1% of indirect causes during the pandemic (Table1).

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12939-025-02588-y/tables/1)

During the pandemic biennium, there was an excess of 283 maternal deaths (44.8%) compared to the pre-pandemic biennium. This proportional excess mortality was higher among older age groups (e.g., 16% among mothers aged 15–19 years vs. 72.6% among those aged 40–49 years), mothers with higher education levels, Andean ethnicity, no prenatal care, a birth plan, and primigravidas (Table1).

Maternal deaths from direct causes remained relatively stable over time, while deaths from indirect causes increased significantly during 2020 and 2021 (Additional file 1, Figure S1A). Notably, two major peaks in maternal mortality were observed during the COVID-19 pandemic: one in May 2020 and another in March, April, and May 2021. These spikes coincided with periods of heightened general COVID-19 mortality in the country. Indirect causes of maternal mortality increased, with the monthly average rising from 8.6 deaths (SD: 3.2) in 2018–2019 to 13.3 (SD: 5.6) in 2020, reaching 18.3 (SD: 12.3) in 2021 (Additional file 1, Figure S1B).

### Association between MMR and determinants

Bivariate analysis revealed statistically significant associations between MMR and proximal determinants (MCM and SBA) as well as distal determinants (UBN and GDP per capita). An increase in SBA, MCM, or GDP per capita was associated with a reduction in MMR, whereas an increase in UBN was associated with a rise in MMR. In multivariate analysis, only SBA and UBN maintained statistically significant associations with MMR after adjusting for other indicators in the model (Table2). The final multivariable negative binomial mixed-effects model showed good explanatory power, with substantial contributions from both fixed effects and contextual random effects (region and year) (Additional file 1, Table S6).

During 2010–2014, the national average MMR was 78.7 per 100,000 live births, and the absolute inequality gradient (measured by the SII) was 78.7 excess maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in the most disadvantaged region compared to the most advantaged region. During 2015–2019, the national average MMR decreased to 65, while absolute inequality increased to 85.3 per 100,000. In 2020–2021, the national average MMR rose to 83.4, with absolute inequality reducing to 75.3 per 100,000. A similar pattern of temporal change was observed in the relative inequality gradient, measured by the CIx.

The MMR consistently remained highest in the most socially disadvantaged quintile based on UBN across all periods analyzed (Fig.2A and B). When considering only the extreme UBN quintiles, the absolute gap in MMR remained nearly unchanged between pre-pandemic and pandemic periods (68.1, 66, and 65), while the relative gap decreased (2.5, 2.8, and 2.0). For 2010–2014, this indicated an excess of 68 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in the most disadvantaged quintile compared to the most advantaged quintile, with a 2.5-fold higher maternal mortality risk in the disadvantaged quintile.

Figure2C and G illustrate the social gradients in MMR and SBA coverage, respectively, using regression slopes derived from linear models where regions are ranked by UBN. These slopes represent the direction and magnitude of inequality across the full socioeconomic spectrum: a steeper negative slope indicates greater disadvantage among lower-ranked regions, while flatter slopes suggest more equitable outcomes. These patterns are consistent with the inequality indices presented in Table3, ensuring alignment between visual and numerical representations.

SBA coverage improved progressively at the national level (87.1%, 93.6%, and 95%) and in terms of absolute (SII: 30.6%, 22.8%, 14.9%) and relative inequalities (CIx: 6.3%, 3.6%, 2.4%) between regions, even during the pandemic period, as well as in the gaps between extreme UBN quintiles.

## Discussion

Our study documents the progressive reduction in maternal mortality in Peru between 2010 and 2019, when it reached its lowest level, and its subsequent increase during the COVID-19 pandemic, culminating in 2021 with levels surpassing those recorded in 2010. The study also highlights the persistent gradients of inequality in maternal mortality, disproportionately concentrated in the country’s most socially disadvantaged regions (pro-rich pattern), and identifies SBA and UBN prevalence as key ecosocial determinants.

The decline in the MMR observed between 2010 and 2019, a reduction of 32.2% over the period and 4.2% annually, reflects Peru’s remarkable progress in maternal and child health, including reductions in neonatal mortality, under-five mortality, and child malnutrition. These improvements are linked to sustained multisectoral poverty reduction programs and active civil society participation [26,27,28]. However, this favorable and enduring trend starkly contrasts with the sharp increase in MMR during the COVID-19 pandemic, representing a setback of at least a decade, primarily attributable to excess maternal mortality from indirect causes associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Excess maternal deaths appear to be a ubiquitous outcome of COVID-19 [29], driven by both the direct effects of the virus and the disruption of healthcare services [30, 31]. The increase in indirect causes of maternal mortality, particularly SARS-CoV-2 infection, underscores the vulnerability of pregnant women during global health crises [12, 29]. In the Americas, reported excess maternal mortality ranged from 12.6% in Colombia [32], 46.3% in the United States [33], and 56.8% in Mexico [34] to 71.6% in Brazil (35.3% in 2020 and 103.3% in 2021) [35] and 92% in Chile [36], with variability depending on the reference baseline and observation period. Our study found a 44.8% excess maternal mortality during the pandemic biennium (2020–2021) compared to the immediate pre-pandemic biennium (2018–2019).

Although the epidemiological profile of maternal deaths remained consistent across the two periods– concentrated among women aged 30–39 years, with low education levels, of Mestizo ethnicity, in unpaid occupations, receiving prenatal care, lacking a birth plan, and multiparous– excess maternal mortality was concentrated among women aged 40–49 years, with higher education levels, of Andean ethnicity, without prenatal care, with a birth plan, and primigravidas. This contrast may reflect both the direct effects of the virus and the indirect consequences of healthcare service disruptions. A longitudinal ecological study across Peru’s 25 regions in 2020, using decomposition methods, identified COVID-19 incidence, per capita income, and unemployment rates as primary drivers of excess mortality, emphasizing the influence of socioeconomic determinants [37].

It remains to be documented whether the multisectoral poverty reduction programs that contributed to the declining MMR during the pre-pandemic decade were adversely affected during COVID-19. A thematic analysis of available evidence highlights the role of structural determinants, political economy, state–society relationships, and vested interests in shaping policy options during this period [38].

An important– and nuanced– finding from our study is that the favorable downward trend in MMR from 2010 to 2019 observed at the national level was not accompanied by an equally downward trend in the within-country poverty-related inequality in maternal mortality. While the national-level decline in maternal mortality is encouraging, the persistence– or even worsening– of inequality within regions highlights ongoing inequities, either structural and/or in access to care and resources. If the poverty reduction programs were not sufficiently targeted, it might indicate that broader economic improvements did not translate into equitable health gains for marginalized populations. The inverse equity hypothesis– where initial health improvements benefit wealthier groups first [39]– could also be playing a role.

The marked pro-rich gradient in maternal mortality across Peru’s regions– and its persistence over time– is a well-documented ecosocial characteristic in Peru and other Latin American countries [5,6,7,8, 14, 32, 35]. This pattern indicates, even at an ecological level and with limited granularity, the role of social determinants in health inequalities. These inequalities in maternal mortality, and by extension in its proximal determinants, result from inequities in the distribution and fulfillment of basic life and health opportunities across individuals, populations, and territories [40].

In contrast to pre-pandemic years, during the pandemic period, inequality gaps and gradients in MMR narrowed, coinciding with a generalized increase in MMR across all regions and ecosocial strata. Notably, the annualized rate of increase in MMR between 2015 and 2019 and 2020–2021 was higher in the quintile of regions with the lowest UBN (from 37.8 to 64.7 per 100,000, an annual increase of 15.4%) compared to the quintile with the highest UBN (from 105.2 to 131.0 per 100,000, an annual increase of 6.3%). In other words, during the COVID-19 pandemic, an upward leveling (leveling up) of the MMR inequality gradient was observed, rather than the anticipated downward leveling (leveling down). This undesirable effect, clearly visible in inequality regression curves, raises questions about the effectiveness of social protection measures targeting the most vulnerable territories during the pandemic.

The generally favorable trends in the proximal determinants of maternal mortality– SBA, modern contraceptive use, and adolescent pregnancy rates– are notable. These trends are observed both at the national average level and in reduced interregional inequalities by UBN.

On one hand, they suggest a modest and temporary disruption in healthcare services during the pandemic, at least at the macro level. On the other hand, they reflect significant advancements in access to and quality of prenatal care and reproductive health services over recent decades.

These improvements are supported by training programs for healthcare personnel. They emphasize obstetric emergency management in rural areas with limited medical services. Additionally, intercultural approaches have been adopted to provide culturally sensitive care, especially for Indigenous populations [26,27,28, 41, 42].

Our study presents important limitations, mainly related to its ecological design and low data granularity. The absence of individual-level measurements prevents the formulation of causal inferences from the results; however, its orientation toward exploratory data analysis allows for the identification of potentially useful patterns to inform public health decision-making [43]. Low granularity underrepresents the expected variability of the studied phenomena at more local levels; nevertheless, the main health phenomenon analyzed (i.e., maternal death) is– fortunately– a statistically rare event, and its study therefore usually requires aggregation at broader territorial levels and/or temporal pooling. This same low granularity may lead to underestimation of the magnitude of ecosocial inequalities, thus generating, in any case, conservative hypotheses. Health indicators such as SBA, MCM, and AFP are based on data from ENDES, a household survey that uses probabilistic sampling and self-reported information. While ENDES is a valuable and widely used source for monitoring population health indicators, it is not exempt from limitations such as recall bias and potential underreporting, particularly at the social extremes. These limitations may affect the precision and comparability of the estimates, potentially leading to underestimation of inequalities. Even so, its methodological rigor, regular implementation, and temporal comparability provide a solid foundation for the analysis conducted. Another limitation is the absence of relevant variables on maternal health, which restricts the comprehensiveness of the study and limits the analytical exploration of determinants and inequalities. Additionally, data quality represents a potential source of bias, particularly due to the underreporting and misclassification of maternal deaths. In this regard, it is noteworthy that for the estimation of maternal deaths, the capture-recapture method is systematically used to correct underreporting based on notifications from the national surveillance system and the vital statistics registry [17]. Nonetheless, residual underreporting and classification errors persist, usually more frequent in socially disadvantaged regions, which could lead to underestimation of mortality and artificially attenuate inequality gradients. Furthermore, official estimates are reported only as annual totals, without disaggregation by direct or indirect causes, which limits the ability to construct reliable cause-specific mortality trends. In addition, during the initial periods of the pandemic, significant challenges arose in the accurate coding and classification of COVID-19–related deaths, which may have affected the correct attribution of indirect causes in some cases of maternal mortality. However, it should be noted that in 2021 an official update of the number of COVID-19 deaths was implemented in Peru [18]. This update contributed to reducing classification biases and improving the accuracy of the figures used in studies such as the present one.

### Future research directions

Research on social inequalities in maternal health should delve deeper into high-quality administrative data with granular disaggregation by key dimensions of inequality, including residence, education level, wealth, and ethnicity, to inform more targeted and effective interventions to eliminate unjust inequalities. It is crucial to adopt approaches that examine the intersectionality of inequality dimensions to identify the most vulnerable population groups. Additionally, qualitative research is essential to explore structural barriers and mechanisms that generate and perpetuate inequalities in accessing healthcare during pregnancy and childbirth. Evaluating the impact of maternal health policies on equity is equally important, focusing on identifying the most effective strategies to reduce inequalities. To improve data quality and strengthen surveillance systems, it is recommended to adopt the methodology of the Intentional Search and Reclassification of Maternal Deaths (BIRMM, by its Spanish acronym), which helps identify and correct misclassified or underreported maternal deaths and should be institutionalized as part of routine monitoring [44]. Finally, institutionalizing the monitoring of these inequalities is essential. This is necessary not only to identify inequities and advocate for political action to promote equity but also to build accountability mechanisms. These mechanisms are crucial to uphold the collective commitment to leave no one behind [45]. They also help calibrate the efforts needed to meet the ambitious maternal health goals of the 2030 Agenda [46].

## Conclusions

The risk of maternal mortality in Peru has progressively and significantly declined over the years. However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the MMR rose to levels observed before 2010. This increase was primarily driven by a rise in indirect causes associated with SARS-CoV-2. Ecosocial inequality in MMR remains high. Maternal mortality continues to be disproportionately concentrated in socially disadvantaged regions, with no significant improvement since 2010. In contrast, SBA coverage has steadily increased. It has maintained high levels even during the pandemic and has helped narrow inequality gaps and gradients across regions. At an ecological level, this evidence highlights the importance of actions targeting proximal determinants of maternal mortality. It also underscores the urgent need for intensified social reforms to positively influence distal determinants in the country.

## Data availability

This analysis utilized publicly available data collected by third parties. The datasets from Peru’s National Institute of Statistics and Informatics are publicly accessible through their data repositories. However, access to maternal mortality data requires submitting a formal request to Peru’s National Center for Epidemiology, Disease Prevention, and Control.

## Abstract

### Background

Maternal mortality is a global public health priority, with the Sustainable Development Agenda and the Sustainable Health Agenda for the Americas setting ambitious targets for its reduction by 2030. Despite progress in poverty reduction and increased life expectancy, Peru faces urgent health challenges, including persistently high maternal mortality, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. To analyze maternal mortality trends and epidemiological characteristics in Peru, explore its determinants during 2010–2021, and quantify its inequalities before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

### Methods

An ecological study used administrative data from the 25 Peruvian regions (2010–2021). Maternal mortality ratio (MMR) trends and key characteristics were analyzed. A mixed-effects negative binomial regression model assessed associations between MMR and proximal (e.g., skilled birth attendance [SBA]) and distal (e.g., unmet basic needs [UBN]) determinants. Inequality trends in MMR and SBA coverage were evaluated using standard metrics.

### Results

MMR declined from 82.0 to 55.6 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births between 2010 and 2019 but rose to 86.7 in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Excess maternal mortality during 2020–2021 (44.8%) was concentrated among older mothers, primiparas, and those without prenatal care, with indirect causes playing a major role. The reduction in MMR (2010–2019) correlated with decreased UBN and increased SBA. Ecosocial inequalities in MMR remained significant, with maternal mortality disproportionately affecting regions with higher UBN (78.7, 85.3, and 75.3 excess deaths per 100,000 live births in 2010–2014, 2015–2019, and 2020–2021, respectively). SBA coverage improved nationally, narrowing regional inequalities from a 30.6-point deficit in 2012 to 14.9 in 2021.

### Conclusions

Maternal mortality in Peru declined significantly before 2020, but the COVID-19 pandemic reversed this progress, with MMR rising to pre-2010 levels. Ecosocial inequalities persist, disproportionately affecting disadvantaged regions. However, SBA coverage improvements highlight the impact of proximal determinant interventions. Strengthened social reforms targeting distal determinants are crucial to reducing maternal mortality and inequalities in Peru.

## Background

Maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is one of the key indicators of public health, reflecting the overall effectiveness, accessibility, and equity of health systems. Reducing maternal mortality has been a global priority for decades. The third Sustainable Development Goal of the 2030 Agenda aims to reduce the MMR to less than 70 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births globally by 2030 [1]. In the Americas, the Sustainable Health Agenda 2018–2030 has adopted an even more ambitious target of less than 30 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030, with an explicit focus on closing equity gaps that disproportionately affect the most vulnerable women [2].

Despite these commitments, recent estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO) indicate that maternal mortality has hardly declined since 2015. At the current pace, the world is off track to meet the established goal, and the global MMR would be more than double the SDG target [3]. This critical situation is mirrored in the Americas region [4]. National averages often obscure significant social and health inequalities. Studies in some countries in the Americas have explored trends and inequalities in maternal mortality and its proximal determinants– such as prenatal care, skilled birth attendance, and postnatal care– using spatially disaggregated administrative data and/or surveys. These studies invariably reveal profound and persistent socioeconomic inequalities in maternal mortality, even amidst national-level improvements in the MMR [5,6,7,8].

In Peru, maternal mortality remains a serious public health concern, particularly among socially disadvantaged populations [9, 10]. Social inequalities, such as poverty, rural residence, and ethnic background, continue to restrict equitable access to essential maternal health services. The COVID-19 pandemic has further exacerbated these inequalities [11], directly through increased maternal morbidity and mortality related to infection [12], and indirectly through widespread disruptions in maternal health services [13]. These disruptions have likely amplified preexisting barriers to care, including lack of transportation, shortages of trained personnel in rural and Amazonian regions, and financial constraints.

Although Peru achieved substantial progress during the Millennium Development Goals era, reducing its national MMR from 88.5 per 100,000 live births in 2001–2003 to 68.7 in 2012–2015, and narrowing regional inequality gaps by over 50%, significant disparities persisted [14]. In the context of COVID-19, the extent to which these inequalities have widened or changed remains insufficiently studied.

Despite persistent inequalities and the recent disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, there is still a lack of updated and systematic analyses in Peru that assess how the key epidemiological patterns and inequities in maternal mortality have evolved over time. This study aims to describe the trends and key epidemiological characteristics of maternal mortality in Peru, ecologically explore its determinants during 2010–2021, and quantify inequalities within the country before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

## Methods

### Study design, variables, and data sources

This study employed a case series and ecological design. The case series included individual records of maternal deaths from the epidemiological surveillance system of Peru’s National Center for Epidemiology, Prevention and Disease Control (CDC-Peru). Maternal death was defined as the death of a woman of reproductive age (15–49 years) while pregnant or within 42 days of pregnancy termination, regardless of the pregnancy duration or location, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes [15, 16]. Case series variables included calendar year, age, education level, cause of death, ethnicity, occupation, prenatal care, birth plan, and primigravidity.

The MMR was defined as the ratio of maternal deaths to live births in the country, region, or specific geographic area during a given calendar period, expressed per 100,000 live births. Annual estimates of MMR and maternal deaths at the national and subnational levels (regional territories) were calculated using the capture-recapture method [17], incorporating data from Peru’s epidemiological surveillance system and vital statistics registry. COVID-19–related mortality analysis utilized data from the CDC-Peru epidemiological surveillance system. For the classification of indirect maternal deaths associated with COVID-19, the technical criteria established for the identification of COVID-19–related deaths were applied in accordance with WHO recommendations [18, 19].

The ecological analysis considered the 25 territorial regions of Peru as the units of analysis. Variables included in the exploratory analysis – besides calendar year, live births, and MMR – were the proportion of women of reproductive age using modern contraceptive methods (MCM), the proportion of adolescent mothers or first-time pregnant adolescents (AFP), and skilled birth attendance (SBA) as proximal determinants of maternal mortality. Additionally, the prevalence of unmet basic needs (UBN) and gross domestic product (GDP) per capita were included as distal determinants. Data on MCM, AFP, and SBA were obtained from official reports published by Peru’s National Institute of Statistics and Informatics (INEI), derived from the Demographic and Health Survey (ENDES) [20]. ENDES is a nationally representative survey that uses a complex, stratified, multistage sampling design based on household self-reports. SBA was defined as the proportion of live births attended by qualified health personnel (physician, obstetrician, or nurse), and INEI reported no changes in its definition for the period 2010–2021. Data on UBN and GDP were obtained from publicly available official estimates provided by INEI.

### Data analysis

Trends in annual national estimates of MMR and its proximal and distal determinants from 2010 to 2021 were analyzed. The epidemiological characteristics of maternal deaths during the pandemic biennium (2020–2021) were compared with those of the pre-pandemic biennium (2018–2019) using chi-squared or Fisher’s exact tests, depending on sample size and expected frequencies. Additionally, for each variable category, the proportional excess maternal mortality during the pandemic biennium was calculated using the standard formula analogous to the attributable fraction:

$$\begin{array}{l}\:excess\:maternal\:deaths\:\left(\%\right)\:=\\\:\frac{\left({{deaths}_{pandemic}\:-\:{deaths}_{prepandemic}}_{}\right)}{{deaths}_{prepandemic}}\times\:100\end{array}$$

A mixed-effects negative binomial regression model was used to examine the ecological association between MMR and proximal and distal determinants for the 2010–2019 period, excluding pandemic years to avoid disruptions in MMR trends. The multivariable analysis included random effects for region and year to control for unobserved variability. Prior to model fitting, we assessed multicollinearity among explanatory variables using the variance inflation factor (VIF), computed from an ordinary least squares regression model. Predictors with VIF values greater than 5 were reviewed for potential redundancy. SBA, identified a priori as a key variable, was retained in the final model after confirming its VIF was within acceptable limits and that its inclusion did not compromise model stability (Additional file 1, Table S5).

Inequality analyses utilized UBN as an equity stratifier. A household is considered poor by UBN if it meets at least one of the following criteria: (1) inadequate housing conditions, based on wall and floor materials and housing type; (2) overcrowding, defined as more than 3.4 persons per room; (3) lack of any type of sanitation; (4) presence of at least one child aged 6–12 not attending school; or (5) high economic dependency, defined as households with a head of household with incomplete primary education (up to second grade) and either (i) four or more persons per employed household member, or (ii) no employed members at all [21, 22]. Regional MMR data were consolidated into three periods (2010–2014, 2015–2019, and 2020–2021) for stability, while SBA data corresponded to 2012, 2017, and 2021. Four standard inequality summary metrics were calculated: absolute gap, relative gap, slope index of inequality (SII), and concentration index of inequality (CIx), following WHO’s established methodology [23]. The absolute gap represents the difference between the weighted mean of the most disadvantaged quintile and that of the most advantaged; higher values indicate greater absolute inequality, while values close to zero reflect greater equity. The relative gap was presented as a ratio between these same quintiles; values greater than 1 indicate a disproportionate burden in the most disadvantaged group, while values less than 1 reflect a greater burden in the most advantaged group. The SII, estimated through weighted regression, represents the absolute difference in the health indicator between the most advantaged extreme (social position 1) and the most disadvantaged (social position 0); a negative value indicates that the health indicator is higher in regions with worse social position, while a positive value indicates a greater burden in the more advantaged regions. The CIx summarizes the relative inequality across the entire distribution of the stratifier, where negative values indicate concentration of the health indicator in the most disadvantaged regions, and positive values in the most advantaged [24]. The SII was calculated using weighted regression with a negative binomial model for MMR and a logistic model for SBA, as these models showed better fit based on mean squared error. Data analyses were performed using the R programming language, version 4 [25].

### Ethical considerations

This study did not involve human participants; only secondary, anonymized, and publicly accessible data were used. Therefore, ethical committee approval was not sought.

## Results

### Trends in maternal mortality and its determinants

Figure 1 illustrates the trends in the MMR and some of its proximal and distal determinants from 2010 to 2021. Between 2010 and 2019, the estimated MMR in Peru exhibited a declining trend, dropping from 82 to 55.6 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, with a marked reduction between 2015 and 2016 (from 76.5 to 59.7). Prior to the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in 2015, the MMR decreased by 8% during 2010–2014, with an average annual reduction rate of 1.6%. Subsequently, a more significant reduction of 20.9% was observed between 2015 and 2019, with an average annual reduction rate of 4.18%. However, this trend reversed during the pandemic years, with the MMR rising to 86.7 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2021 (Fig.1A). A similar pattern was observed in the trends for adolescent pregnancy (Fig.1C) and UBN (Fig.1F). In contrast, SBA (Fig.1B), modern contraceptive prevalence (Fig.1D), and GDP per capita (Fig.1E) showed upward trends during the same period, with a temporary decline in 2020 (and SBA in 2021).

### Epidemiological profile of maternal mortality and excess mortality during the pandemic

The proportional distribution of maternal deaths by age, education level, ethnicity, occupation, prenatal care, birth plan, and gravidity was statistically identical between the pre-pandemic biennium (2018–2019) and the pandemic biennium (2020–2021). Overall, maternal mortality was concentrated among women aged 30–39 years, with low education levels, of Mestizo ethnicity, in unpaid occupations, receiving prenatal care, lacking a birth plan, and multiparous. Hypertensive disorders and obstetric hemorrhages were the leading direct causes of maternal death in both periods, accounting for 76.3% and 77.9% of direct causes, respectively. Deaths linked to COVID-19 infection represented 56.1% of indirect causes during the pandemic (Table1).

During the pandemic biennium, there was an excess of 283 maternal deaths (44.8%) compared to the pre-pandemic biennium. This proportional excess mortality was higher among older age groups (e.g., 16% among mothers aged 15–19 years vs. 72.6% among those aged 40–49 years), mothers with higher education levels, Andean ethnicity, no prenatal care, a birth plan, and primigravidas (Table1).

Maternal deaths from direct causes remained relatively stable over time, while deaths from indirect causes increased significantly during 2020 and 2021 (Additional file 1, Figure S1A). Notably, two major peaks in maternal mortality were observed during the COVID-19 pandemic: one in May 2020 and another in March, April, and May 2021. These spikes coincided with periods of heightened general COVID-19 mortality in the country. Indirect causes of maternal mortality increased, with the monthly average rising from 8.6 deaths (SD: 3.2) in 2018–2019 to 13.3 (SD: 5.6) in 2020, reaching 18.3 (SD: 12.3) in 2021 (Additional file 1, Figure S1B).

### Association between MMR and determinants

Bivariate analysis revealed statistically significant associations between MMR and proximal determinants (MCM and SBA) as well as distal determinants (UBN and GDP per capita). An increase in SBA, MCM, or GDP per capita was associated with a reduction in MMR, whereas an increase in UBN was associated with a rise in MMR. In multivariate analysis, only SBA and UBN maintained statistically significant associations with MMR after adjusting for other indicators in the model (Table2). The final multivariable negative binomial mixed-effects model showed good explanatory power, with substantial contributions from both fixed effects and contextual random effects (region and year) (Additional file 1, Table S6).
